name: Terpene combination (oral essential-oil preparation for urinary stones)
short: Trials of an oral terpene (essential-oil) preparation for kidney or ureter stones: mild-to-moderate drug-related events (7 in 4 people vs 2 in 2 on placebo); gut upset in 7 of 43 in another.
text: This entry covers an oral terpene (essential-oil) preparation, taken as capsules or tablets, used for kidney and ureter stones; the trial abstracts name one branded product but do not list its ingredients; the 2013 meta-analysis below lists the ingredients of a terpene compound drug that it does not name. In a 222-person placebo-controlled trial after shock-wave lithotripsy, 9 mild-to-moderate adverse events were judged drug-related (7 events in 4 people on the terpene combination, 2 in 2 people on placebo); in a 100-person randomized trial after lithotripsy, no complications or differences in symptoms and signs between the groups were reported; in an 87-person double-blind trial for ureteric stones, 7 of the 43 people on the preparation had mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal disturbances and no other significant side effects were noted in either group; and in a 40-person double-blind trial in acute renal colic, no significant side effects were noted with the preparation. In a study after shock-wave lithotripsy in which 150 people took the preparation and 70 took antispasmodic medicines (the abstract does not say how patients were allocated), blood counts and biochemistry did not differ significantly between the groups and all values were normal; the authors' conclusion says the treatment was not accompanied by complications or side effects, and the abstract gives no adverse-event counts. A 2013 meta-analysis of five trials (344 people) of a terpene compound drug, which it describes as pinene, camphene, borneol, anethole, fenchone and cineol in olive oil (the abstract does not name a product, so it may not be the same preparation), reported only minor gastrointestinal adverse effects. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
